newsitem.title: GERMANY: Frankfurt to grow but cannot beat London - lobbyists.
newsitem.headline: Frankfurt to grow but cannot beat London - lobbyists.

text.p: Frankfurt will not replace London as Europe's top financial centre but has every chance of a more powerful role once the Euro currency is launched, a high-profile lobby group for the German city said on Wednesday.

"London will retain its full strength as a financial centre after EMU, of that I am convinced," Rolf Breuer, co-founder of the newly-formed group, said, referring to European economic and monetary union.

But Breuer, future chairman of Germany's top bank Deutsche Bank AG, told a news conference: "Germany's financial centre is better than its reputation. Our aim is to have Germany join the premier league of financial centres worldwide."

Modelled on a successful French initiative, the lobby group -- called Finanzplatz or literally "financial centre" -- aims to generate debate and push for changes to help Germany improve its standing as the 1999 launch date for the common European Union currency approaches.

Brushing aside common "myths" about German financial markets' illiquidity, lack of sophistication and laxity on insider dealing, Breuer said markets here were dynamic and innovative enough to withstand stiff competition.

"The German bond market is one of the biggest in the world, our futures and options exchange (DTB)is one of the most modern and competitive around and our processing systems are also among the best in the world," he said.
Breuer challenged a common complaint from foreign players that German banks, not least the giant Deutsche Bank itself, had almost total control on the stock market.

Just under half of turnover on the DTB and a third of transactions on the IBIS electronic share trading system are controlled by foreign banks -- a sign that the German market is far more open than many of its competitors, he said.

Moreover the recent Deutsche Telekom flotation, Europe's biggest ever with a planned total volume of some 20 billion marks ($13 billion), would help ease the German market's perenniel problem with liquidity, he said.

Such virtues, and not least Frankfurt's future position as home to a European Central Bank, should propel the city into a prime location for issuers, investors and banks, given continued efforts to improve the range of products on offer and eliminate tax disincentives for investment here.

But Breuer, who currently heads Deutsche Bank's global investment banking activities, also said London's capital markets had advantages in terms of personnel and experience which Frankfurt could not hope to rival.
"I would recommend that all banks should conduct at least part of their capital markets activities from London," he said.

As with other major German banks, Deutsche now conducts the vast bulk of its investment banking business via its British unit -- Deutsche Morgan Grenfell -- a move which Bonn once described as a "slap in the face" for Frankfurt.

Breuer, on the other hand, applauded German legislators and the Bundesbank for their support in boosting Frankfurt's cause through new financial markets legislation, tighter market supervision and a more conciliatory monetary policy.

He noted in particular the Bundesbank's decision last week to partially ease its much-derided minimum reserve requirements, which call on banks to hold non-interest bearing deposits with the central bank to cover certain transactions and are regarded as a costly competitive disadvantage.
"Many of our wishes have been realised," Breuer said, while adding: "That is not to say we are at an end."

Breuer warned that if the Bundesbank succeeded in having minimum reserves in their current form adopted by the European Central Bank, financial centres in the Euro region could find themselves at a sharp disadvantage compared with London if Britain remains outside the currency union.
"But I am confident it will not come to that," he said, predicting that a compromise could be reached.
